gtm_strategy_seo.title: Build and lock the GTM strategy onboarding flow
gtm_strategy_seo.prompt:
Use the attached DOZ requirements prompt as the governing requirements source and the attached first-output prompt as the starting draft. Reconcile both attachments before writing anything. If they conflict, preserve the explicit DOZ requirement and report the conflict instead of guessing.

Build the Onboarding Form for [client board]. Read the existing Client settings, product workspaces, Maturity Axis, Product Evolution, Positioning and channel selections first. Reuse those records as the source of truth; do not create duplicate company, product, industry, market-axis or channel data. Preserve unrelated tabs, products and existing strategy work.

Complete the Onboarding Form sequentially and lock each confirmed step: (1) Products; and (2) Market system. The company identity remains in Client settings; do not create a separate Company onboarding step. Do not create standalone GTM Setup, Industries or Channels steps. Put Business / offer type, Single Industry or Multi Industry with its industry name fields, Primary GTM goal, and PLG or SLG sales motion together in the right-hand question panel of Market system. Do not create a separate Primary ICP onboarding step. A locked answer remains editable later, but downstream steps must not silently overwrite it.

PRODUCTS
Add between one and three named products. Do not invent product names. For each product, preserve or enter the supplied source text, description, notes or other onboarding context in that product's text area; never generate missing product copy. Mark exactly one product as active; that product controls the active Product Architecture, Maturity Axis, Positioning and Keywords workspace. Keep every other product workspace and its product text intact.

MARKET SYSTEM
Treat the selling component/buying component choice, the compact GTM question panel and the 4x4 market matrix as one step, not separate tabs or canvases. Keep the puzzle aligned left, place the questions to its right, and place the full matrix below them. Choose exactly one selling axis and one buying axis from Technology, Process, People and Input. Use the compact B2B/B2C switch to review the correct market and examples for every intersection, then select the exact intersection only when supported by the supplied company and product evidence. Use the existing Maturity Axis industryMode, industries and activeIndustry fields as the one source of truth, and project those industries into the Positioning Canvas as industry vertical tabs with the edit pencil on the left and industry tabs plus the add tab on its right. Save the same axes and B2B/B2C context to Product Evolution and Positioning so all three views agree.

MARKET MAP
The Market map step shows one dot per country (Client markets) × company size (Enterprise, Mid-market, Small business) the client picked. Place every dot before the client sees it; the client only drags the ones they disagree with. Read the segments with onboarding_market_map_get, then save with onboarding_market_map_set. x is buyer awareness, from 0 (least aware of the problem and the solutions) to 1 (most aware). y is value delivered, from 0 to 1: what the product gives that segment minus what the buyer pays and expects. Base each placement on the product, the buying axis and the evidence for that country and company size, not on the app's rough built-in estimate. Never move a dot the client placed (source "you") unless the client asks; the tool skips those and reports them.

RESEARCH > GTM STRATEGY
Manage Channels outside the Onboarding Form in the dedicated Research > GTM Strategy page. Choose Inbound, Outbound or both, then select the actual channels used. Inbound can include AEO, SEO, Listicle Outreach, Reddit and any user-supplied channel. Outbound can include Email, LinkedIn, ABM and any user-supplied channel. Do not mark an unused channel merely because it exists in the template.

If AEO is selected, explicitly choose the applicable workstreams: AI visibility and citation audit; prompt and answer monitoring; entity and topical authority; answer-ready content; citation and mention building; and schema and technical readiness. Use only workstreams supported by the plan. Keep SEO and AEO distinct while showing how they reinforce each other. Preserve the same shared channel records when editing them from Research > GTM Strategy.

OUTPUT AND SAVE RULES
First produce a concise proposed Onboarding Form summary for review: company, 1-3 products with the active product and supplied product text identified, Single Industry or Multi Industry with all supplied industry names, B2B/B2C context, selling axis, buying axis and selected matrix intersection. Report inbound/outbound choice, selected channels and selected AEO workstreams separately as Research > GTM Strategy. After approval, update the existing onboarding, GTM Strategy and shared source records. Do not create or display a separate dotted GTM strategy canvas beneath the onboarding flow. Guard against concurrent edits, save only this client board, and verify that locked steps, product count, active product, product text, business or offer type, primary GTM goal, sales motion, industry mode, industry names, market context, market axes, selected channels and AEO workstreams persist after reload.

keyword_supporting_processes.title: Route supporting-process keywords into one workspace
keyword_supporting_processes.prompt: For every client and product, Keywords must contain one aggregate Supporting Processes workspace beside the selected pillar-process workspaces. Read the selected Maturity Axis first. Do not create a separate keyword toggle for each supporting node. Move every keyword, topic and URL whose primary subject is an actual supporting process into the one Supporting Processes workspace, while preserving awareness stage, ICP or Value destination, AEO or SEO mode, article type, URL ownership, metrics, status and decisions. Remove the moved record from the pillar-process workspace so it is not duplicated. Pillar-process content remains in its own selected-node workspace. For the AI Data Platform, data collection, data ingestion, normalization, data integration / ETL, connectors, storage and data warehousing are supporting-process subjects; Reporting and Analysis are pillar-process subjects. Problem Unaware > Value, Problem Aware > Value and Solution Aware > Value use the same process-by-department Value AEO structure, but each stage stores independent content. Copy only the structure from Solution Aware; never copy its keywords, URLs, titles, statuses or other cell values into another stage. Preserve and restore the destination stage's own existing URLs, keywords and metadata, and archive its prior view before restructuring. Existing Problem Unaware and Problem Aware Value SEO source records must be projected into the new process-by-department structure without relabelling, deleting or copying them across awareness stages; place every URL under its semantic process, department and Process/Output/Outcome/Benefits/Tools lens. The awareness cards and lens badges must count the populated projected cells, not raw repository URL records. Available article types include Guides, How-to articles, Explainers, Trends and Topic vs Topic in addition to the established types.

maturity_technology_cards.title: Name technology cards by type and list examples
maturity_technology_cards.prompt: In the Maturity Axis, keep the operational process name as structured process metadata for routing, but display a technology card using the technology type as the visible node name. Put concrete tools, vendors or people only in Who or what does it?. Do not use a vendor pair such as Looker or Tableau as the node name. Example: visible node BI / reporting platform; process Reporting; Who or what does it? Looker / Tableau / Triple Whale / Daasity / Analyst. Preserve actor ownership and exactly two Features or Skills. Apply this rule to existing boards and future clients without inventing vendors.

positioning_document.title: Positioning Document — shared rules
positioning_document.prompt:
The Positioning Document has one AI prompt per section. Open the AI Prompts button on the section you are filling — Positioning (with separate prompts for ICP, Category, Competitive and Value Positioning), Awareness Messaging Framework, Offers, Distribution Plate, Trust Signals or Perception and Framing — and use that section's prompt. Every section prompt carries these shared rules:

Work on [product] on [client board]. Confirm the active product first. Internally read the selected ICP, the selected category, the competitive stages, the problems with their evidence, the value rows (including those marked as USPs) and the Product Architecture. Use XYZ wherever the subject company needs to be named; keep the product name separate. Do not rename the client or replace competitors' identities in underlying data.

Write concise, self-contained final copy: no canvas references, internal IDs, source links, citations, reviewer names, review counts, sample-size discussion or research-process commentary. Evidence stays internal and gives direction. Keep claims logical — problem → specific capability → how it works → benefit — and do not invent shipped functionality, technologies, customer results, superiority or numbers. A proposed architecture is not proof of delivery; where needed, qualify a proposed capability once rather than repeating disclaimers.

Update only this section of the active product's Positioning Document. Preserve every other section, internal evidence, source metadata, other tabs and products. Guard against concurrent edits and verify the saved result.

positioning_canvas.title: Research and fill the Positioning Canvas
positioning_canvas.prompt:
Fill the requested sections of the Positioning Canvas for [product] on [client board] in [market]. Confirm the active product, read its Product Architecture and current selections, and preserve unrelated work and other products. If ICP/category are unselected, map the options first and leave selection to the user.

ICP CARD MODEL
Create exactly one ICP card per Maturity Axis row, in the same order and named after that maturity level (for example "L3 - Qualification"). Every row shows four axes: People, Process, Input and Technology. The buying axis chosen in onboarding (usually Process) is locked: it is carried over from the matching Maturity Axis row and is never written on the canvas. The other three describe what that process requires, the way the car someone drives tells you the house they live in: Technology is the technographics needed to run that process; Input is the volume, quality and types of data the process needs; People maps the department that runs the process, by job designation. Start with a Department line: the department's name, its typical total headcount at this maturity level and who it reports to, sized to that row's Firmographic Proxies. Then list every job designation inside the department, one block per role: the title, how many people typically hold it (a range), their seniority and core skills, and a one-line JD of what that role does in this process (for example "Data Analyst — 1–3 · mid-level, 2–5 years (SQL, Excel, a BI tool) / JD: answers department heads' questions on why a number moved"). List only people inside the department, not company-wide firmographics. Segments such as industries, company types or sales motions appear at every maturity level, so they are not separate ICP cards. USE CASE LEVELS: below the four axes, the card's Use Cases table classifies each use case from the market down to the click, one row per use case, across five levels, and every cell states the use case at that level, never a bare label: Industry (the where: name the industry and what companies in it use the product for), Department / Function (the who: name the team and what it uses the product for), Business Process (the what: the specific workflow, problem or objective), Persona / User (the individual: name the role and what that person does with the product and why) and Interaction / Scenario (the how: the step-by-step sequence of inputs, actions and outputs, with the happy path and at least one edge case). The third row holds Buying Trigger (what makes them start looking now), Firmographics (industry, company size, region, activity volume; one line per industry when they differ) and Economic Buyer (who owns the budget and signs off; one line per industry when they differ). The user selects one card, normally the maturity level the product serves; do not select on their behalf. FILL DEPTH: only the ICP card that matches the Maturity Axis row selected (ticked) on the Maturity Axis is filled completely: its four axes, every Use Cases row on all five levels, Buying Trigger, Firmographics and Economic Buyer. Every other card gets its first row only (People, Process, Input and Technology) and leaves Use Cases, Buying Trigger, Firmographics and Economic Buyer as they are, so research credits go to the level being targeted. Never erase content that is already there. If no Maturity Axis row is selected, ask which level to fill completely before writing. Do not create independent icpChoices, grouped table subcolumns or stage canvases.

Categories: map the solution families serving these ICPs, including primitive substitutes. Explain overlaps rather than imposing fixed headcount boundaries. Distinguish software from outsourced services. Competitive positioning: research current peers in the selected category and give each a concise architecture description. Group architectures into evolution patterns on the relevant axis; vendors can span patterns. End with our proposed position, but verify our actual capabilities before claiming superiority or uniqueness.

Problems and evidence come BEFORE values. Research actual customer accounts in review sites, forums/Reddit, interviews or accessible video transcripts, not training-data guesses, AI review summaries or vendor marketing presented as customer evidence. Require at least FIVE distinct reviewer/organisation accounts supporting each retained problem. Deduplicate the same person, reposts and syndicated reviews; five URLs repeating one account count once. Prefer selected-ICP/market matches and multiple platforms/vendors. Record a direct link (review author/date locator if no permalink), a short paraphrase, date, ICP fit, incentive/affiliation if known, and whether the issue was resolved. Do not infer prevalence from five accounts or claim different reviewers necessarily represent different organisations.

Separate BASELINE problems the category already addresses from REMAINING GAPS. For basics, use five customer accounts describing the prior burden or the benefit of an existing solution; label these solved/table-stakes needs, not current dissatisfaction or unique differentiation. For gaps, require five accounts of the actual remaining difficulty. Merge, narrow, add or remove problems based on evidence; retain weak leads separately as unvalidated, never fabricate evidence to hit five. Do not claim every product solves a basic equally well.

For each retained problem create one linked value row: functional = what we do; benefit = what the customer gets; monetary = the economic mechanism, not invented savings; strategic = downstream business impact. Label proposed capabilities and inferred benefits; distinguish parity from differentiation. Mark every value row that is a genuine differentiator as a USP (isUsp: true); several values can be USPs, but never mark parity or table-stakes values. Preserve selections unless asked to change them and do not modify Keywords or other sections without instruction. Save evidence and values to the active product, verify at least five distinct accounts per problem and one-to-one value links, and warn about stale open-board saves before external updates.

maturity_axis.title: Map departmental process maturity
maturity_axis.prompt:
Build the Maturity Axis for [product] on [client board]. First identify one department and its core raw material or input; maturity describes that department's operating capability, not the size or maturity of the whole company. Read and preserve the current Maturity Axis unless replacement is requested.

Above the maturity rows, add separate Departments and Industries rows. List only relevant names as simple buttons. Store whether the product is Single Industry or Multi-industry. In Single Industry mode, activeIndustry is the only industry used by the solution matrix. In Multi-industry mode, every listed industry becomes a group with the same department columns beneath it. Never invent an industry. AI Data Platform uses E-commerce as its single industry. Do not add raw material, input types, descriptions, maps or nested product sections.

Create one row per successive transformation of the core input. A new maturity begins only when the input is changed into a materially new decision-ready form. Keep earlier transformations in later rows when they remain necessary. Use as many or as few rows as the domain requires; for the AI data platform, use Reporting, Analysis, Forecasting and Optimization. The user may select one maturity, or occasionally two; do not select on their behalf. When the user chooses a maturity row, use replacementSelected only for the exact nodes/processes they intend to replace; never infer these selections merely from a blue current-pillar color.

Draw the operational pipeline in every row. A PILLAR PROCESS directly transforms the input. Mark the newest or most advanced pillar in that row as CURRENT (blue), and previously established pillars repeated from earlier rows as INHERITED (yellow). A SUPPORTING PROCESS enables the maturity but does not directly transform the input; mark it gray. Do not classify a process from importance alone: use its direct effect on the input.

For every node record: (1) a short process name; (2) Supporting or Pillar and, for a pillar, Current or Inherited; (3) T for technology, P for person, or T/P when either or both can perform it; (4) the actual technology, tool, role or person; (5) Features when the actor is technology, Skills when the actor is a person, or Features / skills for mixed ownership. Store exactly two short, concrete items on every node; do not repeat the process name. A process may also contain an editable subProcesses list. Use it only for genuine forms of work inside that process, not upstream supporting steps or downstream outputs. For Analysis, include descriptive, diagnostic, cohort, funnel, attribution, segmentation, retention and churn, customer lifetime-value, product and SKU performance, marketing performance, revenue and profitability, anomaly and trend, root-cause and comparative analysis.

Connect nodes in operational order and name what moves between them. Show parallel sources as separate nodes before ingestion, and keep delivery or decision surfaces explicit. For the AI data platform, map the supplied operation pipeline faithfully: L1 Reporting; L2 Reporting plus Analysis; L3 Reporting, Analysis and Forecasting; L4 Reporting, Analysis, Forecasting and Optimization. Preserve the supplied source systems, ingestion/storage and actors, then give every technology two features and every person two skills.

Lay every canvas out spaciously. Leave at least 280px of clear horizontal space between connected nodes so each connector label is fully readable with room to spare, and at least 80px of clear space between stacked nodes. Keep a single workflow or maturity row on one horizontal line and widen its canvas to the right as far as it needs; never wrap one flow onto a second line to save space.

FIRMOGRAPHIC PROXIES: every maturity row has a small Firmographic Proxies card in its top-left corner. Fill firmographicProxies on each row: revenue (the annual revenue band that typically signals a company running the department at this maturity), employees (the company headcount band, and where it helps, the size of the team that runs the process) and segment (smb, mid_market or enterprise). These are proxies: they suggest the maturity, they do not define it. Derive them from the roles, tools and data volume the row needs. Keep every node at x 226 or more wherever its y is below 252, so no node covers the card.

Save only the active product's Strategy Maturity Axis using maturity_axis_set. Preserve other products and tabs, guard against concurrent edits, and verify Departments, Industries, industryMode, activeIndustry, selected maturity rows, explicitly selected replacement processes, sub-processes, colors/roles, T/P ownership, two features or skills per node and labelled connections after saving.

product_architecture.title: Build a product architecture
product_architecture.prompt:
Build the Product Architecture for [product] on [client board], using [product URL] and [target market, if known]. Read the existing architecture first and preserve existing work unless replacement is requested.

Research official product pages and documentation for this product and comparable software. Consolidate the relevant capabilities into a proposed software-module architecture. Distinguish native capabilities, external integrations and optional extensions; do not imply the product already supports every researched feature.

Create one adjustable row per workflow; the workflow itself is the process. Use only Technology and People nodes, with short, specific names. Give every technology exactly two concrete features and every person exactly two concrete skills. Show people only where someone supplies input, reviews or approves. Put input data and output names on connectors, not separate data or process nodes.

Mark every external system the product connects to but does not own, such as a CRM, calendar, email or third-party data provider, with integration: true. It renders with an Integration badge and does not count as part of the product architecture. Leave the product's own modules unmarked, and never present an integration as a native capability.

Under each workflow keep two fields. Capabilities: one line per capability, naming the node or combination of nodes that delivers it and what it lets the customer do, written as "Node A + Node B: plain-language outcome". Features: the product features in that workflow, grouped by node, with integrations labelled as integrations. Write both for a buyer, not an engineer. Keep every workflow canvas the same height.

Arrange each workflow left to right. When one input feeds parallel technologies, stack those technologies vertically and group them under a common name. Connect their results to a shared destination or separate destinations as appropriate. Keep real dependencies in sequence, and connect related workflows. Leave enough space for readable nodes and connector labels.

Lay every canvas out spaciously. Leave at least 280px of clear horizontal space between connected nodes so each connector label is fully readable with room to spare, and at least 80px of clear space between stacked nodes. Keep a single workflow or maturity row on one horizontal line and widen its canvas to the right as far as it needs; never wrap one flow onto a second line to save space.

Save to the Strategy Product Architecture workflow editor using product_architecture_set, not the older generic canvas. Attach a concise feature/source map to Grounded Evidences, distinguish researched facts from proposed design, and verify the saved nodes, groups and labelled connections.

positioning_document_core.title: Positioning — statement and USP
positioning_document_core.prompt:

ICP Positioning, Category Positioning, Competitive Positioning and Value Positioning each have their own AI prompt; read whatever is already saved in those four fields first and make the statement and USP agree with them. If one of the four is still empty, write it with its own prompt before writing the statement.

Positioning Statement: who XYZ serves, the category of solution and the specific problem, mechanism and benefit, in one or two sentences. It is a sentence about the product's primary axis of evolution.
USP: state the single most defensible, buyer-relevant reason to choose XYZ over realistic alternatives, covering every value row marked as a USP on the canvas. Tie it to a specific mechanism and outcome; do not invent uniqueness or proof.

Work on [product] on [client board]. Confirm the active product first. Write concise, self-contained final copy: no canvas references, internal IDs, source links, citations, reviewer names, review counts, sample-size discussion or research-process commentary. Evidence stays internal and gives direction. A proposed architecture is not proof of delivery; where needed, qualify a proposed capability once rather than repeating disclaimers.

positioning_document_messaging_framework.title: Awareness Messaging Framework — one brief per awareness level, written for the economic buyer
positioning_document_messaging_framework.prompt:
Write the Awareness Messaging Framework for [product] on [client board]: one brief for each awareness level — Problem unaware, Problem-aware, Solution-aware, Category-aware and Competitor-aware. Replace a level only when asked or when it no longer matches the selected ICP.

READ FIRST. Build every brief from the board, not from general marketing knowledge:
- The selected ICP card on the Positioning Canvas: Economic Buyer, Firmographics, Buying Trigger, People, Process, Technology, Input and the Use Cases rows.
- The ticked Maturity Axis row: its process, the roles and tools in it, the nodes marked for replacement, and its Firmographic Proxies card (revenue, employees, SMB / mid-market / enterprise).
- The problems with their evidence, the value rows (and which are USPs), the selected category and the competitive stages.

WHO YOU ARE WRITING FOR. Write for the economic buyer of that ICP at that maturity level — the person who owns the budget and signs off — and name the rest of the buying group where it matters: the champion who feels the problem daily, the validator who checks the money (usually finance), and the likely blocker (often the person whose work the product changes). Use the buyer's own operating language: their P&L lines, headcount plan, current tools, weekly meetings and the decisions they make. A buyer at a mid-market company with an analyst team is not a founder doing everything alone; match the seniority, team and stack on the card.

THE STATUS QUO IS THE CURRENT MATURITY ROW. The real competitor at every level is the process the buyer runs today — the people and tools in their maturity row — and the option of hiring another person into it. The gap to sell is between that process and the work the product takes over (the nodes marked for replacement). Make the cost of staying put concrete: time, money, decisions made late or blind.

VOICE. Write as a senior strategist briefing a content team. Plain, specific, commercial. Every sentence should be something the buyer would recognise from their own week. Explain mechanisms rather than stacking adjectives.
Do not write imagined inner-voice quotes, cute rhetorical questions, dramatic one-liners or slogans. Do not use hype, fear, or filler words such as "quietly", "seamless", "unlock", "game-changer" or "supercharge". Do not invent statistics, customers, trial terms or security claims; write "needs proof" or "confirm before claiming" instead. Do not lead with AI or with roadmap capabilities.

FIELDS FOR EACH LEVEL, in this order, as labelled plain-text lines:
Reader — the buyer and the buying group at this level, with their role, company stage and situation.
Current belief — what they hold true about the problem and their current setup.
The shift — the one belief this level must change to move them one level forward.
Message job — what content at this level must achieve.
Core message — one or two sentences XYZ wants them to take away, in their language.
Angles — three headline-style angles a writer can build a piece on: specific and testable, not slogans or questions for effect.
Proof — the evidence, value rows or customer stories to use; "needs proof" where none exists.
Objections — the objections this level raises, each with its answer (required for Solution-aware, Category-aware and Competitor-aware).
Content and CTA — the formats that fit, matched to the Keywords awareness pages, and the smallest next step.
Avoid — what breaks this level.

WHAT EACH LEVEL MUST DO:
Problem unaware — they believe their current process has it covered. Make one cost of that process visible and measurable from their own operation. No product, company or category.
Problem-aware — they feel the pain but blame the wrong cause (usually capacity: "we need another hire" or "a better dashboard"). Name the structural cause, price it in their terms, and give them a way to put it to whoever signs off. The category may appear at the end only as a concept.
Solution-aware — they know the kind of solution exists and doubt it works for a company like theirs. Show the operating after-state through one peer at the same stage, in outcomes, with one proof point. XYZ may be named.
Category-aware — they are choosing between approaches. Give evaluation criteria that fit their stage and team, explain the trade-offs fairly, and position XYZ as replacing work or tools they already pay for, with time to first value explicit.
Competitor-aware — they are weighing XYZ against a named rival, their current tool or the next hire. Differentiate on mechanism, answer the named objections, offer a low-risk measurable first step, and give the champion a one-page case for the validator: what it replaces, what it costs, what it compares against and when it pays back — as a formula, not an invented figure. Compare on fit; never disparage rivals.

Keep each level self-contained, roughly 250–450 words. Before saving, check every level against the voice rules and remove any sentence the economic buyer would find vague, childish or generic.

Work on [product] on [client board]. Confirm the active product first. Internally read the selected ICP, the selected category, the competitive stages, the problems with their evidence, the value rows (including those marked as USPs) and the Product Architecture. Use XYZ wherever the subject company needs to be named; keep the product name separate. Do not rename the client or replace competitors' identities in underlying data.

Write concise, self-contained final copy: no canvas references, internal IDs, source links, citations, reviewer names, review counts, sample-size discussion or research-process commentary. Evidence stays internal and gives direction. Keep claims logical — problem → specific capability → how it works → benefit — and do not invent shipped functionality, technologies, customer results, superiority or numbers. A proposed architecture is not proof of delivery; where needed, qualify a proposed capability once rather than repeating disclaimers.

positioning_document_framing.title: Perception and Framing — ideal brand perception and frames
positioning_document_framing.prompt:
Write Perception and Framing for [product] on [client board]: the Ideal Brand Perception, then the framing frames. The Ideal Brand Perception says what perception XYZ wants in the buyer's mind; the frames say how XYZ will build it.

Ideal Brand Perception. Write it as plain, readable paragraphs that tell anyone reading it exactly what XYZ wants to be known for — no headings, labels, bullet lists or "Earned by" lines. Open with one sentence on where XYZ wants to sit in the buyer's mind. Then a paragraph on the brand level: the universal traits every company must earn, such as trustworthy, reliable and quality, saying in concrete terms what each one means for XYZ. Then a paragraph on the capability level: the traits XYZ wants to be known for, tied to what buyers judge this kind of solution on (for example most accurate or fastest) and to XYZ's actual capabilities; name first the trait the category is judged on first. Choose only traits that a capability, feature or proof point can support. If a trait still lacks public proof, say so in one closing sentence as a direction, not a claim. Leave out mood words such as calm, bold or friendly that no capability can prove.

Frames. Write the frames in this order: brand-level frames, one for each universal trait in the Ideal Brand Perception; then Category Framing, Problem Framing and Competitive Framing; then capability-level frames, one for each capability trait. Label each frame with its level and the trait or subject it builds (for example "Brand-level framing — trust" or "Capability framing — accuracy"). Each frame is two to four sentences: what the buyer should compare XYZ against, why that comparison builds the trait, and what the buyer should measure or test. Never disparage rivals. Preserve any user-added frames; when asked to change one frame, update only that frame.

Work on [product] on [client board]. Confirm the active product first. Internally read the selected ICP, the selected category, the competitive stages, the problems with their evidence, the value rows (including those marked as USPs) and the Product Architecture. Use XYZ wherever the subject company needs to be named; keep the product name separate. Do not rename the client or replace competitors' identities in underlying data.

Write concise, self-contained final copy: no canvas references, internal IDs, source links, citations, reviewer names, review counts, sample-size discussion or research-process commentary. Evidence stays internal and gives direction. Keep claims logical — problem → specific capability → how it works → benefit — and do not invent shipped functionality, technologies, customer results, superiority or numbers. A proposed architecture is not proof of delivery; where needed, qualify a proposed capability once rather than repeating disclaimers.

positioning_document_icp.title: ICP Positioning
positioning_document_icp.prompt:
Write ICP Positioning for [product] on [client board]. Base it on the selected ICP card on the Positioning Canvas and the selected (ticked) row of the Maturity Axis.

Describe the target as a system of four components: People — the roles in the buying department that run or approve the process, how many of them there typically are and what each does; Process — the workflow at the selected maturity level; Technology — the stack that process runs on today; Input — the volume, quality and types of data it needs.
Give the firmographic proxies from the Firmographic Proxies card of the selected Maturity Axis row: the annual revenue band, the employee band and whether the target is SMB, mid-market or enterprise. Present them as signals that suggest the maturity, not as the definition of the ICP; a small team can run an advanced process.
State the buying trigger — what makes them start looking now — and the economic buyer who owns the budget and signs off.
Set both edges. The floor: why systems below the target are not ready (too little volume, or nobody to act on the output). The ceiling: why systems above it are out of reach (what the stack cannot carry yet). Close with who is not a fit, so the ICP works as a filter rather than an aspiration.

positioning_document_category.title: Category Positioning
positioning_document_category.prompt:
Write Category Positioning for [product] on [client board]. Base it on the selected category and the category ladder on the Positioning Canvas.

Sell why this category of solution is the right fit for the ICP. Start from the substitutes the buyer uses today, from the most primitive (spreadsheets, manual work, a hire) upward, and say what each one stops being able to do as the ICP's process matures. Then explain what products in the selected category have in common — typical architecture, technology components and operating processes — and why that shape serves the ICP better than the substitutes. This is migration logic: the reader should understand why to move up to this category, not which vendor to pick.
Discuss shared patterns, not a vendor list or a maturity ranking. Do not imply every vendor has identical capabilities or invent a shared implementation stack.

positioning_document_competitive.title: Competitive Positioning
positioning_document_competitive.prompt:
Write Competitive Positioning for [product] on [client board]. Base it on the competitive stages and architectures on the Positioning Canvas and on the Product Architecture.

Stay inside the selected category: these are rivals, not substitutes. Group the rivals by how their product is built, along the product's primary axis of evolution, and describe each architecture pattern in a sentence. Then explain XYZ's particular approach within the category and the mechanism behind its proposed advantage — what is built differently and what that changes for the buyer.
Do not confuse category benefits with unique differentiation; say plainly where rivals already offer parts of it. Compare on fit for the ICP's system, never disparage rivals, and do not claim superiority the evidence cannot support.

positioning_document_value.title: Value Positioning
positioning_document_value.prompt:
Write Value Positioning for [product] on [client board]. Value positioning states what XYZ is capable of. Build it only from XYZ's own features, the capabilities those features produce, and the use cases and benefits those capabilities create in each department. Never build it from what is wrong in the market: do not describe market problems, criticise other tools or say what competitors lack.

Base it on the Product Architecture (its workflows, nodes and their Features and Capabilities fields), the Departments list on the Maturity Axis, the selected ICP card's Use Cases rows, and the value rows on the Positioning Canvas, giving the rows marked as USPs the most weight. Problems and evidence may tell you which capabilities matter most to the buyer, but they are never written into this section.

Organise the section by capability. For each capability write four labelled parts:
Features: the specific product features and integrations that produce it.
Capability: what those features together let XYZ do, in one or two sentences.
Use cases: one bullet per department from the Maturity Axis that uses this capability, saying what that department does with it. The same capability applied in a different department is a different use case, so list the major use cases across several departments rather than one generic line. Include only departments where the use is real and supported by the features.
Benefit: what the customer gets from the capability, in one sentence; state economic value as a mechanism, never an invented number.

Put USP capabilities first, then the rest. Cover every capability the Product Architecture supports, and merge capabilities that do the same job.
